ed-procedures-l01.q: A patient leaves in a wrist splint. Which single instruction most reduces swelling over the first 48 hours?
choices: Keep the hand below the level of the heart so blood drains out
Keep the hand elevated above the level of the heart
Leave ice on continuously overnight
Rewrap the elastic bandage tighter twice a day
ed-procedures-l01.why: Elevation above the heart lets gravity move fluid out of the hand. Holding it low increases swelling, continuous ice risks a cold injury to skin already under a splint, and tightening the wrap turns the splint into a tourniquet.

ed-procedures-l01.q: You document the pre-splint check as circulation intact, motor intact, sensation intact. What is missing?
choices: The patient's pain score
The brand of splinting material
A time on the finding, and a repeat check after the splint is wrapped
The name of the ordering provider
ed-procedures-l01.why: Circulation, motor and sensation are documented with a time both before and after application, because the whole point is to compare. A pain score, the material brand and the provider name are charted elsewhere and do not detect a tightening splint.

ed-procedures-l02.q: You are about to build an upper extremity plaster splint. How many layers do you plan on?
choices: 3 to 4
8 to 10
ed-procedures-l02.why: Upper extremity plaster is 8-10 layers; 12-15 is the lower extremity number. Three to four is too weak to hold a fracture, and stacking toward 20 or more raises the heat of curing enough to burn skin.

ed-procedures-l02.q: Why is the splint material measured against the uninjured limb first?
choices: The injured limb is swollen so the measurement reads short
Measuring on the injured side means moving the fracture
Hospital policy requires two measurements
Plaster shrinks as it cures and must be oversized
ed-procedures-l02.why: Every time the fracture moves it hurts and bleeds more, so length is taken off the good side. Swelling changes girth, not the length needed; there is no two-measurement rule, and plaster does not shrink meaningfully.

ed-procedures-l03.q: A patient with a 2nd metacarpal fracture needs a gutter splint. What is different about the radial gutter compared with the ulnar gutter?
choices: It covers the ring and little fingers instead
It crosses the elbow at 90 degrees
It runs along the thumb side and needs a hole cut for the thumb
It is applied without any padding between the fingers
ed-procedures-l03.why: The radial gutter is the mirror image on the thumb side, covering the index and middle fingers, and the thumb has to pass through a cut hole. The ring and little fingers belong to the ulnar gutter, neither gutter crosses the elbow, and both need padding between the splinted fingers.

ed-procedures-l03.q: Which patient is appropriately treated with buddy taping rather than a rigid splint?
choices: A stable non-displaced proximal phalanx fracture of the ring finger
A mallet finger with a drooping fingertip
A fifth metacarpal neck fracture
A suspected scaphoid fracture with snuffbox tenderness
ed-procedures-l03.why: Buddy taping suits stable sprains and non-displaced phalanx fractures and lets the finger keep moving. Mallet finger needs the DIP held straight, a boxer's fracture needs an ulnar gutter, and a suspected scaphoid fracture needs a thumb spica.

ed-procedures-l04.q: You are sizing a cervical collar. How is the measurement taken?
choices: By the patient's neck circumference in centimeters
By finger widths from the top of the trapezius to the bottom of the chin
By the patient's height and weight
By the distance from the chin to the sternal notch
ed-procedures-l04.why: Collar size is a vertical measurement, taken in finger widths from the trapezius to the bottom of the chin and matched to the sizing post. Circumference, body size and the chin-to-sternum distance do not correspond to how the collar posts are sized.

ed-procedures-l04.q: An ankle with an unstable fracture is put in a posterior short-leg slab only. What is the problem?
choices: It holds the ankle in too much dorsiflexion
It uses too few layers of plaster to hold any fracture
It still lets the ankle roll side to side without a stirrup
It prevents the toes from being checked
ed-procedures-l04.why: A posterior slab blocks up-and-down motion but not side-to-side roll, so an unstable fracture needs a stirrup added. The slab alone is fine for a sprain, layer count is a separate decision, and toes stay exposed in either build.

ed-procedures-l05.q: A patient on crutches has the handgrips set so the elbows are nearly straight when gripping. What should you change?
choices: Nothing, straight arms transfer weight better
Raise the handgrips so the elbows bend more than 45 degrees
Lower the handgrips to the wrist crease, giving 15-30 degrees of elbow bend
Shorten the whole crutch until the pad reaches the armpit
ed-procedures-l05.why: Handgrips sit at the wrist crease with the arms hanging, which puts the elbows at 15-30 degrees so the arms can push. Straight arms cannot generate lift, deep bend wastes strength, and a pad seated in the armpit is exactly what causes crutch palsy.

ed-procedures-l05.q: A patient with a splinted wrist asks how long the splint is the treatment. What is accurate?
choices: It is usually a bridge to orthopedic follow-up in 3-7 days
It is the definitive treatment and comes off when it feels better
It stays on for 6 weeks without any recheck
It should be removed at home in 48 hours
ed-procedures-l05.why: Most emergency department splints hold the limb until swelling settles and orthopedics decides on casting or surgery, typically within 3-7 days. Self-directed removal or a six-week unmonitored splint both miss the follow-up where the real treatment is chosen.

ed-procedures-l06.q: A clean-edged kitchen knife cut to the cheek is 9 hours old. Why might the provider still close it?
choices: Facial wounds cannot become infected
The face has a rich blood supply, so closure is often reasonable up to about 24 hours
Any wound can be closed up to 72 hours
Bleeding has already sterilized the wound
ed-procedures-l06.why: The face's blood supply lowers infection risk and widens the closure window to roughly 24 hours. Facial wounds absolutely can get infected, there is no universal 72-hour rule, and bleeding does not sterilize anything.

ed-procedures-l06.q: Which part of the wound description most changes the infection risk for a 3 cm wound?
choices: Whether the patient is right or left handed
The exact color of the surrounding skin
Whether it was a clean knife cut or a crush or bite mechanism
The time of day the injury happened
ed-procedures-l06.why: Mechanism drives contamination and tissue damage: crush and bite wounds get infected far more often than a clean cut of the same size. Handedness, skin color description and clock time do not change bacterial load.

ed-procedures-l07.q: A provider asks for 1% lidocaine with epinephrine for a scalp repair. Which benefit matters most here?
choices: It works instantly with no onset time
Vasoconstriction keeps a very vascular field dry enough to see
It eliminates the need for irrigation
It allows the wound to be closed under tension
ed-procedures-l07.why: The scalp bleeds hard, and epinephrine constricts vessels so the edges are visible; it also extends duration and raises the maximum safe dose. Onset is still 2-5 minutes, irrigation is never skipped, and no anesthetic fixes tension.

ed-procedures-l07.q: A laceration on the forearm is closed with 4-0 nylon. When should the patient return for removal?
choices: 3-5 days
10-14 days
21 days
Whenever the wound stops hurting
ed-procedures-l07.why: Extremity wounds, especially anything over a joint, come out at 10-14 days because the skin is under tension. Three to five days is the face, where scarring matters most, and pain resolution is not a healing endpoint.

ed-procedures-l08.q: A patient has a splinter of glass in the foot and the X-ray shows it clearly, while a second patient has a wood splinter and a negative X-ray. What does that difference mean?
choices: The wood splinter has already dissolved
X-ray reliably shows glass and metal but usually misses wood, which shows better on ultrasound
Negative X-ray rules out any foreign body
Wood foreign bodies can safely be left in place
ed-procedures-l08.why: Glass and metal are radiopaque; wood usually is not, so a negative film does not exclude it and ultrasound is the better look. Organic material must come out because it drives intense inflammation and infection.

ed-procedures-l08.q: During trephination of a subungual hematoma, at what point do you stop?
choices: After a fixed count of 10 seconds
Only once the hole is wide enough to see the nail bed
The instant blood wells up through the hole
After the patient reports pain
ed-procedures-l08.why: Blood escaping means the nail plate is through and the pressure is relieved, and going further drives the tip into the nail bed. There is no time rule, the nail bed should never be exposed, and the nail plate has no nerves so pain is not the signal.

ed-procedures-l09.q: A post-void residual on the bladder scanner reads 40 mL. How do you interpret that?
choices: Normal; the bladder is emptying adequately
Clear retention requiring catheterization
Equipment failure, since a reading under 50 mL is impossible
An indication for an indwelling Foley
ed-procedures-l09.why: Under 50 mL is a normal post-void residual. Retention concerns start when a patient who cannot void holds 300-400 mL, and a residual over 300 mL is clearly abnormal; a normal scan is exactly what avoids an unnecessary catheter.

ed-procedures-l09.q: Which position is correct for a male patient as you advance a urinary catheter?
choices: Legs bent and apart, penis held against the abdomen
Supine with the legs straight, penis held at about 90 degrees to the body
Side-lying with the knees drawn to the chest
Sitting upright at 45 degrees
ed-procedures-l09.why: Holding the penis at roughly 90 degrees straightens the urethra so the catheter passes. Legs bent and apart is the female position, and side-lying or sitting positions belong to rectal exams and lumbar punctures, not catheterization.

ed-procedures-l10.q: A child has a dried bean lodged in the ear canal. Why is irrigation the wrong choice?
choices: The canal is too narrow to accept fluid
Water makes the bean swell and wedge tighter
Irrigation is only used in adults
The bean would dissolve and be impossible to identify
ed-procedures-l10.why: Organic objects absorb water and expand, making removal harder. Canal size is not the issue, ear irrigation is used in children when appropriate, and identification is not the concern; a possible perforation, tubes, a button battery or an inflamed canal are the other contraindications.

ed-procedures-l10.q: You are setting up for a lumbar puncture. Which position does the provider need?
choices: Supine and flat with the head turned away
Lithotomy with the knees draped
Lateral decubitus with knees to chest, chin down, hips and shoulders stacked square
Prone with a pillow under the abdomen
ed-procedures-l10.why: The curled lateral position opens the gaps between the lumbar spines and keeps the spine unrotated. Supine head-turned is the central line position, lithotomy is a pelvic exam, and prone is not used for an LP.

ed-procedures-l11.q: Which finger injury is splinted with the PIP joint held straight while the DIP is left free to move?
choices: Mallet finger
Central slip injury, or boutonniere
Volar plate injury
Tuft fracture
ed-procedures-l11.why: A central slip injury is splinted across the PIP in extension with the DIP free. Mallet finger is the reverse, splinting the DIP with the PIP free; a volar plate injury gets a dorsal extension block at 20-30 degrees, and a tuft fracture gets a fingertip splint.

ed-procedures-l11.q: A patient is fitted with a CAM boot for a stable foot fracture. What is commonly forgotten at fitting?
choices: The heel must be seated fully back and the other shoe needs a lift to level the hips
The straps are tightened from the toes toward the knee
It goes on directly against bare skin
It must be worn for 24 hours before bearing weight
ed-procedures-l11.why: A boot raises one leg, so an unlevelled gait causes hip and back pain over weeks, and a heel that is not seated back lets the foot slide. Straps run from the ankle outward, braces go over a sock, and a prefabricated boot needs no curing time.

ed-procedures-l12.q: A patient in a fiberglass cast asks when it will be strong enough to lean on. What do you tell him?
choices: Immediately, fiberglass is fully strong when applied
Near full strength in about 30 minutes, and follow the provider's weight-bearing order
Not for 48 hours, the same as plaster
After one week
ed-procedures-l12.why: Fiberglass is rigid in 3-5 minutes and near full strength in about 30 minutes, while plaster needs 24-48 hours before weight bearing. It is never fully strong the moment it is rolled on, and a week is far longer than the material requires.

ed-procedures-l12.q: Which technique keeps a cast saw from injuring skin?
choices: Dragging the blade smoothly along the length of the cast in one pass
Cutting directly over the bony prominences where the cast is thinnest
Cutting in and out, lifting and repositioning, and staying on the flat sides of the limb
Pressing harder so the cut finishes faster
ed-procedures-l12.why: In-and-out cuts on the flat surfaces keep the blade off skin and let it cool. Dragging and pressing build heat and cause burns, and bony prominences are exactly where padding is thinnest and skin is closest to the blade.

ed-procedures-l13.q: The provider asks you to cut the suture after each knot on a facial repair. What length are you aiming for?
choices: 5-10 mm tails, or whatever length the provider states
Flush with the knot
About 3 cm so they are easy to grab at removal
Long enough to tie the sutures to each other
ed-procedures-l13.why: Skin tails are usually 5-10 mm, long enough to grasp at removal and short enough not to poke. Cutting flush risks the knot unraveling, very long tails tangle and irritate, and sutures are never tied to one another.

ed-procedures-l13.q: How is a needle loaded into the needle driver?
choices: At the swage, angled with the curve
About one third of the way back from the swage, at a right angle to the jaws
At the point, so the tip is protected
Anywhere, as long as the lock is engaged
ed-procedures-l13.why: Gripping about a third back from the swage at 90 degrees gives control without bending the needle or dulling the point. Clamping the swage can break the thread free, and clamping the point destroys it.

ed-procedures-l14.q: Tissue adhesive is being applied and a slow ooze of blood keeps appearing at the wound edge. What happens if you continue?
choices: Nothing, glue bonds well through blood
The glue sets faster and holds better
The blood lifts the film off from underneath and the closure fails
The wound will heal without a scar
ed-procedures-l14.why: Glue is a surface bridge that requires a dry, bloodless, tension-free wound. Ongoing bleeding separates the film from the skin, and glue never bonds through blood or moisture.

ed-procedures-l14.q: Where is tincture of benzoin applied when placing adhesive strips?
choices: Inside the wound, to seal the base
On the intact skin 1-2 cm to either side of the wound
Over the top of the strips once they are in place
It is not used with adhesive strips
ed-procedures-l14.why: Benzoin makes the skin beside the wound tacky so strips grip. In the wound it stings and inflames tissue, and painting it over the strips does nothing for adhesion.

ed-procedures-l15.q: A patient is planned for moderate sedation. How is the room prepared?
choices: For moderate sedation exactly, since that is the target
For minimal sedation, to avoid over-preparing
For one level deeper than planned, because patients slide between levels
Only after the first dose confirms how the patient responds
ed-procedures-l15.why: Depth is a continuum and patients regularly go deeper than intended, so suction, bag-valve-mask, monitoring and reversal agents are ready for the next level down. Preparing after the first dose leaves the highest-risk minutes uncovered.

ed-procedures-l15.q: Which sedation agent best preserves respiratory drive and airway reflexes?
choices: Propofol
Ketamine
Midazolam with fentanyl
Etomidate
ed-procedures-l15.why: Ketamine is dissociative and generally preserves breathing and airway reflexes, though laryngospasm in young children and unpleasant emergence in adults are its risks. Propofol causes apnea and hypotension, and midazolam with fentanyl is the combination most associated with respiratory depression.

ed-procedures-l16.q: Where is the suction control chamber commonly set on a chest drainage unit?
choices: -5 cm H2O
-20 cm H2O
-40 cm H2O
It is not set; suction is always wall pressure
ed-procedures-l16.why: Minus 20 cm H2O is the usual setting, delivered by a water column or a dry dial. Turning wall suction up higher only makes the water bubble vigorously and evaporate without increasing the applied negative pressure.

ed-procedures-l16.q: A chest tube separates from its drainage unit while the patient is being moved. What is the immediate action?
choices: Clamp the tube until a new unit arrives
Tape the tube end closed with occlusive dressing
Place the free end into a bottle of sterile water to make a temporary water seal
Reconnect it to the old unit without cleaning
ed-procedures-l16.why: Sterile water restores a one-way seal so air cannot travel back into the chest. Clamping or sealing the tube can build a tension pneumothorax if there is an air leak, and reconnecting a contaminated end risks infection.

ed-procedures-l17.q: Why is the modified Allen test done before a radial arterial line?
choices: To measure the patient's blood pressure in both arms
To check that the ulnar artery can supply the hand if the radial is compromised
To confirm the patient is not on anticoagulants
To locate the radial artery by palpation
ed-procedures-l17.why: The test checks collateral flow: color returning in about 5-10 seconds after the ulnar side is released means the hand has a backup supply. It says nothing about blood pressure, clotting medication, or the exact position of the vessel.

ed-procedures-l17.q: The wrist is positioned for a radial arterial line. What is correct?
choices: Flexed forward over a towel roll
Palm up, extended about 30-45 degrees over a rolled towel and taped
Extended as far as it will go for maximum exposure
Held by an assistant without support
ed-procedures-l17.why: About 30-45 degrees of extension brings the artery close to the surface, while overextension kinks it and makes the stick harder. Flexion buries the vessel, and an unsupported wrist moves at the wrong moment.

ed-procedures-l18.q: A 3-year-old needs an IV in 35 minutes and the skin is intact. Which topical fits the time available?
choices: LET gel, applied into the site
EMLA under an occlusive dressing
LMX-4 liposomal lidocaine, about 30 minutes without a dressing
Nothing works that fast; proceed without topical
ed-procedures-l18.why: LMX-4 works on intact skin in about 30 minutes and needs no dressing. EMLA needs a full 60 minutes under occlusion, and LET is for open wounds, not intact skin.

ed-procedures-l18.q: A parent at the foot of the bed is crying and repeatedly apologizing to the child during a laceration repair. What is the most helpful response?
choices: Ask security to escort the parent out
Give the parent a specific job, such as holding a video at the child's eye level
Ignore it and work faster
Tell the child the parent is upset because the procedure will hurt
ed-procedures-l18.why: A parent with a task becomes part of the distraction rather than a source of fear. Removing a parent escalates the child's distress, rushing makes the repair worse, and narrating the parent's fear to the child amplifies it.

ed-procedures-l19.q: A patient heading to the operating room has a wedding ring that will not come off. What is appropriate?
choices: Leave it and say nothing, since it is only jewelry
Cut it off immediately without discussion
Tape it in place and document it, unless the team directs otherwise
Give it to the first family member you see
ed-procedures-l19.why: Jewelry comes off when it can, and a ring that truly will not come off is taped and documented so the operating room knows. Saying nothing hides a burn and swelling risk, cutting without discussion is not your call, and belongings go on a signed valuables form with a named recipient and time.

ed-procedures-l19.q: Which detail belongs in the verbal handoff to the operating room team?
choices: Your personal opinion of how the case was managed
Last oral intake and the exact time, plus lines, drugs given and pending results
Only the diagnosis and the room number
The patient's insurance status
ed-procedures-l19.why: Handoff covers name, age, procedure, allergies, last intake and time, last vitals, lines, drugs and times, pending results, and anything not yet told to the patient. Opinions and insurance details are not clinical handoff, and diagnosis alone leaves the next team blind.

quiz.q: A 40-year-old has a wrist splint applied for a distal radius fracture. Before the splint you documented a 2+ radial pulse, intact finger movement and normal sensation. Which of these should you document after wrapping?
choices: All three findings again, each with a time
Only the pulse, since it is the most objective
Only sensation, since nerves are the fragile structure
Nothing, because the pre-splint check already covered it
quiz.why: The value of the neurovascular check is the comparison, so all three findings are repeated and timed after application. A pulse alone misses nerve compression, sensation alone misses arterial compromise, and skipping the repeat check removes the safety net entirely.

quiz.q: A 16-year-old with a splinted forearm calls four hours after discharge. His fingers tingle and the tingling does not change when he props the arm on pillows above his chest. What should he be told?
choices: Take ibuprofen and call back in the morning
Come back to the emergency department now to have the splint checked
Loosen the elastic wrap himself and continue to monitor
Apply ice for another 20 minutes and recheck
quiz.why: Numbness or tingling that does not resolve with elevation is a return-now symptom because the splint may be compressing nerve or vessel. Analgesia and ice do not relieve compression, and a patient rewrapping their own splint at home cannot assess what they have done.

quiz.q: A hand is being splinted in the position of function. Which set of angles is correct?
choices: Wrist flexed 20 degrees, knuckles straight, thumb against the palm
Wrist neutral, knuckles bent 30 degrees, thumb straight out sideways
Wrist extended 20-30 degrees, knuckles bent 70-90 degrees, finger joints nearly straight, thumb abducted
Wrist extended 45 degrees, knuckles bent 20 degrees, thumb taped to the index finger
quiz.why: The position of function holds the collateral ligaments at length so the joints do not stiffen in a useless posture. Flexed wrists and straight knuckles are the classic stiff hand, and a thumb held against the palm or taped to a finger loses the grip position entirely.

quiz.q: A tech dips plaster in hot tap water because it speeds up setting. What is the effect on the patient?
choices: Only that the splint is weaker than intended
No clinical effect; only the working time changes
It makes the splint set too slowly to mold
Faster and hotter curing, with a real risk of a thermal burn under the splint
quiz.why: Plaster cures exothermically, so hotter dip water plus thick layers plus insulation has caused full-thickness burns. Water at roughly 20-25 degrees C is the target; the strength issue and slow setting described in the other choices are not what hot water does.

quiz.q: You have just laid a freshly dipped plaster splint on a patient's leg. Where should the limb rest while it cures?
choices: On an uncovered surface, never on a pillow or blanket
On a folded blanket to cushion the heel
On a pillow, to keep it elevated while setting
Wrapped in a warm sheet to speed the cure
quiz.why: Padding under a curing splint traps the heat of the reaction against skin. Elevation matters after the splint has set, not during the cure, and deliberately insulating it is exactly how thermal injuries happen.

quiz.q: An elastic bandage is applied over a finished forearm splint starting at the elbow and wrapping down toward the hand. What is the consequence?
choices: The splint will be too loose to hold the fracture
Swelling is pushed toward the hand and trapped there
The plaster will not laminate properly
No consequence, as long as the tension is even
quiz.why: Wrapping distal to proximal pushes fluid toward the heart; wrapping the other way drives it into the hand where it has nowhere to go. Wrap direction does not affect lamination, and the direction genuinely matters regardless of tension.

quiz.q: A 52-year-old office worker has wrist pain on the thumb side, worse with gripping, and the provider diagnoses de Quervain tenosynovitis. Which immobilization fits?
choices: Long-arm posterior splint
Ulnar gutter splint
Short-arm wrist-based thumb spica
Volar forearm splint with the thumb free
quiz.why: De Quervain involves tendons at the thumb side of the wrist, so a wrist-based thumb spica rests both. A long-arm splint immobilizes far more than needed, an ulnar gutter covers the wrong side of the hand, and a volar splint leaving the thumb free does not rest the inflamed tendons.

quiz.q: A 27-year-old fell on an outstretched hand. The X-ray is normal but she is tender in the anatomic snuffbox. She asks why she needs a splint for a normal X-ray.
choices: It is only for comfort and she may remove it at will
Because the radiologist may have missed a distal radius fracture
Because all wrist injuries are splinted regardless of findings
Because a scaphoid fracture often does not show on film for 10-14 days, and a missed one can lose its blood supply
quiz.why: Scaphoid fractures are frequently occult early and the bone's blood supply enters distally, so a missed fracture risks avascular necrosis. The splint is protective, not merely comfort, and the reason is the known behavior of the scaphoid, not a suspected radiology error or a blanket rule.

quiz.q: A patient has a humeral shaft fracture. The coaptation splint is applied and the tech is ready to discharge him. What is missing?
choices: A sling and swathe
A cervical collar
A posterior long-arm splint added on top
A knee immobilizer for transport
quiz.why: The sling carries the forearm's weight and the swathe stops the arm swinging, and a coaptation splint always gets both. A collar and a knee immobilizer are unrelated devices, and stacking a long-arm splint on top adds weight that works against the gravity traction the coaptation relies on.

quiz.q: A patient in a knee immobilizer after a reduced patellar dislocation asks how long to wear it continuously. What is the important caution?
choices: It must stay on at all times for six weeks without exception
A knee locked straight stiffens quickly, so gentle motion resumes as soon as the provider allows
It should be removed whenever it is uncomfortable
It can be replaced with an elastic wrap after 24 hours
quiz.why: Immobilizers are effective and also stiffening, so the plan is early controlled motion under the provider's direction. Six weeks of continuous immobilization causes avoidable stiffness, comfort is not the criterion for removal, and an elastic wrap provides no stability.

quiz.q: A patient wears a rigid cervical collar for six hours in the department awaiting imaging. What is the specific risk you should be watching for?
choices: Collar-induced airway obstruction from the chin piece
Allergic contact dermatitis to the plastic
Pressure injury at the chin and the back of the head
Loss of collar effectiveness after four hours of wear
quiz.why: Rigid collars cause pressure injuries at the chin and occiput surprisingly fast, so the skin is inspected with two people and manual stabilization. Airway obstruction is a sizing problem from a collar that is too tall, allergy is uncommon, and collars do not expire with wear time.

quiz.q: A posterior short-leg splint with a stirrup is being built for an unstable ankle fracture. What does the stirrup add that the posterior slab does not provide?
choices: Extra layers for overall strength
Padding over the heel
Elevation of the foot above the heart
Control of side-to-side roll at the ankle
quiz.why: The stirrup runs up both sides of the leg under the heel, blocking inversion and eversion that the posterior slab leaves free. Padding, layer count and elevation are separate parts of the job and do not address rotational instability.

quiz.q: A patient with a new forearm splint wants to shower. What do you tell him?
choices: Cover it completely with a waterproof cover or bagged and taped, and keep it dry
Shower normally and dry the splint afterward with a hair dryer on hot
Remove the splint to shower and reapply it after
Wet plaster is fine as long as it is rewrapped
quiz.why: Wet plaster crumbles and wet padding macerates skin nobody can see, so the splint is covered and kept dry. A hot hair dryer burns, removing and reapplying loses immobilization, and a soaked splint has to be changed, not rewrapped.

quiz.q: A patient with a non-weight-bearing right ankle fracture is learning crutches. Which description matches the correct gait?
choices: Both crutches and the right leg advance together, then the left leg steps through
Both crutches advance, weight goes into the hands, and the left leg swings past the crutches while the right never touches down
The right leg advances first, then the crutches follow
The patient alternates one crutch and the opposite leg with both feet contacting the floor
quiz.why: Non-weight-bearing uses a swing-through pattern with the injured leg never contacting the floor. Advancing the injured leg with the crutches is the three-point partial weight-bearing pattern, and any pattern that puts the right foot down violates the order.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old with a painful left hip is given a cane. In which hand does it go and why?
choices: Left hand, so it is closer to the painful side
Either hand, whichever feels natural
Right hand, so the cane and the painful leg advance together and share the load across a wider base
Both hands, using two canes
quiz.why: A cane in the opposite hand moves with the affected leg and offloads it, mimicking normal arm swing. Holding it on the painful side narrows the base and does not unload the joint, and defaulting to whatever feels natural usually produces the wrong side.

quiz.q: A 5 cm laceration has visible grit ground into the base after a motorcycle slide. Irrigation alone has not cleared it. What is appropriate?
choices: Pour povidone-iodine into the wound to sterilize the debris
Close it over the debris and start oral antibiotics
Leave the debris; it will work its way out over weeks
Scrub the area with a brush after adequate anesthesia
quiz.why: Ground-in particles tattoo the skin permanently and are the one situation where scrubbing is justified, after good anesthesia. Antiseptic inside a wound kills healing cells, closing over debris traps infection, and retained particles do not clear on their own.

quiz.q: Your department has run out of sterile saline for irrigation. The provider suggests warm tap water for a simple, clean 3 cm forearm laceration. What is the evidence-based response?
choices: Tap water and sterile saline give the same infection rates in simple wounds, so this is acceptable
Tap water is never acceptable and the wound must wait for saline
Tap water is acceptable only if hydrogen peroxide is added
Tap water is acceptable only for wounds less than 1 cm
quiz.why: Studies show equivalent infection rates for potable tap water and saline in simple wound irrigation. Delaying irrigation raises risk, peroxide is never added to a wound, and there is no size cut-off in the evidence.

quiz.q: You are set up to irrigate and realize you have only a 10 mL syringe and a 25 gauge needle. What is wrong with using it?
choices: It delivers far too little pressure to dislodge bacteria
It delivers pressure well above the 8-15 psi target and drives bacteria deeper
It cannot deliver enough total volume in a reasonable time and is therefore the only problem
Nothing; syringe size does not affect irrigation pressure
quiz.why: A small syringe through a narrow needle generates pressure above the useful range, damaging tissue and forcing bacteria into it. The 8-15 psi target comes from a 35-60 mL syringe through an 18-19 gauge catheter or splash guard, so syringe and catheter size very much matter.

quiz.q: A 60 kg patient is having a large back laceration repaired with 1% lidocaine with epinephrine. What is the approximate maximum volume that can be used?
choices: About 14 mL
About 27 mL
About 42 mL
About 70 mL
quiz.why: The maximum is 7 mg/kg with epinephrine, so 60 kg gives 420 mg; at 10 mg/mL for a 1% solution that is about 42 mL. Roughly 27 mL would be the plain lidocaine limit at 4.5 mg/kg, and 70 mL exceeds the safe dose and risks systemic toxicity.

quiz.q: A patient says she is allergic to lidocaine because the last dental injection made her heart race and her hands shake. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: A true anaphylactic reaction to the amide anesthetic
An allergy to the preservative that requires a different drug class
Lidocaine toxicity from an excessive dose
A reaction to the epinephrine in the anesthetic, not an allergy
quiz.why: Tachycardia and tremor are classic epinephrine effects, and true amide anesthetic allergy is rare. Anaphylaxis presents with hives, swelling and airway compromise, and lidocaine toxicity shows as perioral numbness, metallic taste, confusion and seizures, not a brief racing heart.

quiz.q: A 22-year-old completed her childhood tetanus series and had a booster 3 years ago. She has a deep, dirty laceration from a garden tool. What does she need for tetanus?
choices: Nothing
Td or Tdap only
Tetanus immune globulin only
Td or Tdap plus tetanus immune globulin
quiz.why: With three or more prior doses, a dirty wound needs a booster only if the last dose was more than 5 years ago, and hers was 3 years ago. Immune globulin is reserved for an unknown or incomplete series with a dirty wound.

quiz.q: An abscess is drained and packed with a half-inch iodoform strip at 22:00 on Monday. What must the patient be told before leaving?
choices: The packing will dissolve on its own
The packing is in the wound and must be removed or exchanged in 24-48 hours
The packing can be pulled out at home once it stops draining
The packing prevents any further drainage from the wound
quiz.why: Packing is a wick, documented by length, with a tail left outside, and it is removed or changed at 24-48 hours by a clinician. Plain and iodoform gauze do not dissolve, home removal skips the wound recheck, and the packing exists precisely to keep drainage flowing.

quiz.q: A patient has a tick attached to the shoulder. Which instruction is correct?
choices: Inject lidocaine around the tick so it detaches
Smother it with petroleum jelly and wait
Grasp it at the skin with fine-tipped forceps and pull straight up with steady traction, no twisting
Twist it counterclockwise while pulling
quiz.why: Steady upward traction close to the skin removes the whole tick. Twisting breaks off mouthparts, and smothering or injecting around it prolongs attachment, which matters because time attached drives the Lyme decision.

quiz.q: A wound has heavy serous drainage soaking through gauze every few hours. Which dressing is the best match?
choices: Hydrogel
Dry gauze changed more often
Hydrocolloid
Alginate or foam
quiz.why: Alginate gels as it absorbs and foam holds large volumes, both designed for heavy drainage. Hydrogel adds moisture to dry wounds, hydrocolloid suits light drainage, and simply changing gauze more often macerates the skin and does not manage the exudate.

quiz.q: You are inserting a Foley in a female patient. Urine returns at about 6 cm. The tech beside you says to inflate now so the catheter does not slip out. What is correct?
choices: Advance another 2-5 cm first, then inflate with 10 mL of sterile water
Inflate immediately, since urine confirms bladder placement
Withdraw 2 cm, then inflate
Inflate with 10 mL of normal saline for better balloon stability
quiz.why: Urine return means the tip is in the bladder, but the balloon sits behind the tip, so advancing a few more centimeters keeps it out of the urethra. Inflating a balloon in the urethra tears it, withdrawing makes that worse, and saline can crystallize and jam the deflation channel.

quiz.q: A trauma patient has blood at the urethral meatus and the provider has not yet examined him. A nurse asks you to place a Foley for output monitoring. What do you do?
choices: Place it gently with extra lubricant
Hold the catheter and tell the nurse and provider about the blood at the meatus
Use a coudé catheter instead to avoid the injured area
Place a smaller 12 French catheter
quiz.why: Blood at the meatus suggests urethral injury, and passing any catheter can convert a partial tear into a complete one. A smaller or curved-tip catheter does not make the attempt safe; the attempt stops and a provider decides.

quiz.q: An NG tube is being measured for a 5 foot 8 inch adult. Which measurement determines the insertion depth?
choices: A standard 55 cm for all adults
Chin to sternum, doubled
Nose to earlobe to xiphoid process
Nose to the top of the sternum
quiz.why: The nose-earlobe-xiphoid measurement approximates the distance to the stomach and is marked on the tube before insertion. A fixed number ignores body size, and the shorter landmarks leave the tip in the esophagus.

quiz.q: A worker has an alkali splash from drain cleaner in the right eye. Which single fact most changes your urgency compared with an acid splash?
choices: Alkalis cause more pain, so the patient needs earlier analgesia
Alkalis are more likely to cause an allergic reaction
Alkalis are neutralized by tears within minutes
Alkalis dissolve cell membranes and keep penetrating deeper as long as they are present
quiz.why: Alkali injuries tunnel, so ongoing presence means ongoing damage and irrigation starts immediately, before registration or acuity. Acids coagulate surface protein, which forms a partial barrier. Pain severity is not the deciding factor and tears cannot neutralize a caustic load.

quiz.q: You finish irrigating a chemical eye exposure with 2 liters and the pH strip reads 7.2 the instant the flow stops. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The reading may reflect the irrigation fluid; wait 5-10 minutes and recheck before stopping
The eye is in range and the patient can be discharged
The strip is faulty because 7.2 is impossible after irrigation
Irrigation should continue for another 2 liters regardless of pH
quiz.why: Testing immediately measures the fluid running over the surface, not the eye, so you wait for equilibration and recheck against a goal of 7.0-7.4. Discharging on that first reading can miss ongoing injury, and adding fixed extra volume without rechecking is not how the endpoint is set.

quiz.q: You are assisting at a sterile field during a central line. You need to reach an item on the opposite side of the field. What do you do?
choices: Reach across quickly with hands held high
Walk around the field to the other side rather than reaching across it
Ask the provider to slide the field toward you
Turn your back to the field and reach behind you
quiz.why: Reaching across a sterile field contaminates it, and turning your back means you can no longer see it. Walking around preserves both rules; dragging the field breaks its edges and disturbs the setup.

quiz.q: A patient with an unstable elbow fracture is placed in a posterior long-arm splint with radial and ulnar side struts. What do the struts add?
choices: They shorten the setting time of the plaster
They allow the patient to bear weight through the arm
They block rotation as well as bending
They eliminate the need for padding over the olecranon
quiz.why: Side struts, in effect a double sugar-tong, control supination and pronation that a posterior slab alone cannot. They do not change curing time, do not permit weight bearing, and bony prominences still need extra padding.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old has a proximal scaphoid fracture. The provider asks for a thumb spica that also blocks rotation. Which variation is needed?
choices: Short-arm wrist-based thumb spica
Volar forearm splint with a thumb hole
Ulnar gutter with the thumb included
Long-arm thumb spica crossing the elbow
quiz.why: Only a splint crossing the elbow blocks forearm rotation, which is why a proximal scaphoid fracture gets the long-arm version. A wrist-based spica controls the wrist and thumb but not rotation, and the other two do not immobilize the thumb at all.

quiz.q: A patient with a volar plate injury of the index PIP joint is splinted with the finger held perfectly straight. What is the concern with that position?
choices: The injury needs a dorsal extension-block splint at 20-30 degrees of flexion, not full extension
Full extension is correct and no change is needed
The MCP joints should have been included at 70-90 degrees
The DIP joint should have been splinted instead
quiz.why: A volar plate injury is a hyperextension injury, so the splint blocks the last 20-30 degrees of extension while allowing flexion. Full extension puts the healing volar plate on stretch, and the MCP and DIP positions described belong to different injuries.

quiz.q: An orthopedic resident applies a short-arm fiberglass cast in the department. Which application error is most likely to force the cast to be cut off the same night?
choices: Using stockinette that was cut too long
Rolling the cast material onto the limb under tension
Molding with flat palms instead of fingertips
Applying three layers of cast padding rather than two
quiz.why: Cast material is unrolled and allowed to lie on the limb; pulling it tight makes the cast a tourniquet on a swelling extremity. Extra-long stockinette is folded back by design, flat palms are the correct molding technique, and three layers of padding is within the normal 2-3.

quiz.q: A short-arm cast is bivalved for pain and numbness, yet nothing improves. The cast shells spread but the limb is still tight. What was most likely missed?
choices: The bivalve should have been a univalve
The patient needs a tighter elastic wrap over the shells
The cast padding underneath was not cut
The arm needed to be lowered below the heart
quiz.why: Intact cotton padding still encircles the limb and holds pressure, so the padding is cut with blunt-tipped scissors after spreading. A univalve relieves less, not more; tightening the wrap recreates the problem; and lowering a swollen limb increases pressure.

quiz.q: Which patient is at the highest risk of a cast saw burn during removal?
choices: An alert adult with a two-week-old fiberglass forearm cast
A teenager with a plaster cast applied yesterday
An anxious adult who asks a lot of questions during removal
A sedated patient whose cast crosses several bony prominences
quiz.why: Saw burns happen when nobody can report heat, and bony prominences are where padding is thinnest. An alert patient, including an anxious one, will tell you the instant something feels hot, and cast age or material is not the driving risk.

quiz.q: A provider asks for forceps to hold the skin edge during a facial repair. Which do you hand over?
choices: Adson forceps with teeth
Smooth-jawed dressing forceps
A hemostat
Skin hooks passed tip-up
quiz.why: Toothed Adson forceps grip skin with less crush than smooth jaws, which have to squeeze harder to hold. Smooth forceps are for suture and gauze, a hemostat crushes tissue, and skin hooks are sharp and are passed tip-down.

quiz.q: A provider is draining an abscess and asks for a blade. Which one should you have ready?
choices: A 10 blade
An 11 blade
A 15 blade
A 20 blade
quiz.why: The 11 blade has a sharp point made for stabbing into an abscess and drawing a small incision. A 15 blade is for fine curved cuts, a 10 blade for longer incisions, and a 20 blade is for large surgical incisions, not a bedside drainage.

quiz.q: During a repair, the provider hands you the needle driver with the needle still loaded and turns to get more suture. What is the correct action?
choices: Set it on the drape and say nothing to avoid breaking concentration
Unload the needle and drop it in the sharps container immediately
Announce the sharp out loud, keep it controlled, and place it where it was agreed
Hand it to the nurse standing behind you
quiz.why: Every sharp is announced out loud every time it moves, and it stays controlled so the count holds. A silent handoff is how needlesticks happen, discarding a needle mid-repair destroys the count and the field, and passing it to a third person off the field compounds the risk.

quiz.q: Staples are being removed from a 10 cm abdominal wound placed nine days ago. At the mid-point the skin looks thin and the edges are just beginning to separate. What is reasonable?
choices: Remove all staples and apply a dry dressing
Leave all staples in for another week without evaluation
Remove all staples and close the thin area with tissue adhesive
Remove every other staple, lay adhesive strips across, and arrange a recheck
quiz.why: Staggered removal with strip support keeps tension off a fragile wound while allowing a planned recheck. Removing all of them invites dehiscence, leaving them all without evaluation ignores a warning sign, and glue never goes on a wound under tension.

quiz.q: A patient returns two days after a sutured forearm laceration. There is 1 cm of redness at the wound edge, no warmth, and the pain has been improving daily. Temperature is 36.9 C. What does this represent?
choices: Normal inflammation at the wound edge
Early cellulitis requiring antibiotics
Lymphangitis
Dehiscence
quiz.why: A narrow 1-2 cm rim of redness with no warmth and settling pain is expected healing. Infection brings spreading redness, warmth, increasing pain or pus; lymphangitis shows a streak up the limb, and dehiscence means the edges have separated.

quiz.q: A 4 cm laceration repaired five days ago has partly opened, with clean granulating tissue visible at the base and no pus. The patient asks you to tape it closed. What is correct?
choices: Tape the edges together firmly and discharge him
Expose it, measure it, document what is visible at the base, and have a provider see it before anything is closed
Apply tissue adhesive across the separation
Irrigate with hydrogen peroxide and then tape it
quiz.why: A dehisced wound is assessed and documented before anything seals it, because closing over old or contaminated tissue traps the problem inside; many are left to heal from the base with strip support. Peroxide never goes in a wound, and glue on a separated wound under tension will fail.

quiz.q: During a sedation, the patient's end-tidal CO2 number climbs from 38 to 58 mmHg while the waveform stays present and the saturation reads 98%. What does this mean?
choices: Complete apnea
Normal recovery from sedation
Hypoventilation, which is the warning that comes before apnea
A sampling line disconnection
quiz.why: A preserved waveform with a rising number means the patient is breathing but not enough, so intervene now with stimulation and airway positioning. A flat trace is apnea, a disconnection loses the waveform entirely, and the saturation on supplemental oxygen is not reassuring.

quiz.q: A patient is 25 minutes past the last dose of propofol, awake, oriented, saturating 97% on room air, with a blood pressure 8% below baseline. The Aldrete score is 9. What does this indicate?
choices: The patient must remain for a full 2 hours regardless
Sedation monitoring may stop immediately at any score
Flumazenil should be given to complete the recovery
Recovery criteria are largely met, though monitoring commonly runs about 30 minutes after the last dose
quiz.why: An Aldrete of 9 or more with vitals within about 20% of baseline is a common discharge threshold, with roughly 30 minutes of monitoring after the last dose. A rigid 2-hour rule is not standard, monitoring is not stopped on score alone, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not propofol.

quiz.q: A patient is being sedated for a hip reduction and the provider asks the monitoring nurse to help pull traction on the leg. What is the correct response?
choices: The monitoring person cannot take on another task; a different person must pull traction
Helping is fine as long as the monitor alarms are on
Helping is fine because the reduction takes less than a minute
The monitoring person may help if capnography is in place
quiz.why: The dedicated monitor has one job, because deterioration during sedation is fast and quiet. Alarms, short duration and capnography all help, but none of them replaces a person whose eyes are on the patient and the monitor.

quiz.q: Joint fluid from a knee aspiration is thick, cloudy and yellow-white, and print cannot be read through it. What should you anticipate?
choices: It is normal joint fluid and the tap can be discarded
Urgent handling for possible septic arthritis, with prompt delivery of the culture and cell count tubes
The fluid should be reinjected into the joint
The specimen can wait until the next lab courier run
quiz.why: Normal synovial fluid is clear and straw-colored; cloudy or purulent fluid raises septic arthritis, which destroys cartilage in days. Aspirated fluid is never reinjected, and a delayed cell count degrades and becomes unusable.

quiz.q: A chest tube is being placed for a simple pneumothorax. Which detail about needle and tube path prevents vascular injury?
choices: Entering below the nipple line at the anterior axillary line
Entering at the second intercostal space in the midclavicular line only
Passing over the top of the rib below rather than under the rib above
Angling the tube toward the diaphragm
quiz.why: The intercostal artery, vein and nerve run in a groove under the lower edge of each rib, so the tube rides on the top of the rib below. The safe triangle is bounded below by the nipple line, not entered beneath it, and tube direction is chosen for air or blood, not vessel safety.

quiz.q: A patient has a chest tube draining a pneumothorax. The water seal chamber shows fluid rising and falling with each breath and no bubbling. How do you interpret this?
choices: There is a large air leak requiring immediate attention
The unit is broken and must be replaced
Suction is set too low and should be increased
The system is patent and there is no current air leak
quiz.why: Tidaling means the tube is open to the pleural space, and the absence of bubbling means air is no longer escaping. Bubbling, not tidaling, indicates a leak; neither finding suggests equipment failure or a need to change the suction setting.

quiz.q: During a lumbar puncture the provider asks which interspace is being targeted and why it is safe. What is accurate?
choices: L3-L4 or L4-L5, which is below where the spinal cord ends at about L1-L2 in an adult
L1-L2, which is where the subarachnoid space is widest
T12-L1, located off the lower rib margin
S1-S2, because the sacral space is largest
quiz.why: The cord ends at roughly L1-L2, so entering at L3-L4 or L4-L5, located off the iliac crest line, avoids it. Higher interspaces risk the cord itself, and the sacral segments are fused with no accessible interspace.

quiz.q: Cerebrospinal fluid tube 1 shows 3,200 red cells per microlitre and tube 4 shows 3,050. What does this pattern suggest?
choices: A traumatic tap that is clearing
Blood present in the cerebrospinal fluid itself, consistent with subarachnoid hemorrhage
A laboratory dilution error
Normal cerebrospinal fluid
quiz.why: Blood from the needle washes out between tubes 1 and 4, so counts that stay essentially unchanged point to blood that was already in the fluid. A clearing count is the traumatic tap pattern, and normal fluid contains virtually no red cells.

quiz.q: An arterial line transducer has drifted 10 cm below the phlebostatic axis. How does the displayed pressure change?
choices: It reads about 7.5 mmHg too low
It is unaffected if the system was zeroed earlier
It reads about 7.5 mmHg too high
The waveform flattens completely
quiz.why: A transducer below the reference point sees extra hydrostatic column, roughly 7.5 mmHg per 10 cm, and reads falsely high; above the axis reads falsely low. An earlier zero does not correct later movement, and leveling error changes the numbers, not the waveform shape.

quiz.q: A 6-year-old is about to have an IV placed and asks whether it will hurt. What is the best response?
choices: Tell her it will not hurt at all so she stays calm
Avoid the question and start immediately
Explain every step in detail 20 minutes beforehand
Tell her honestly that it will feel cold and then like a pinch, right before you start
quiz.why: Age-appropriate honesty right before the procedure preserves trust and reduces distress; promising no pain destroys trust the moment the needle goes in. A long wait after an explanation is its own torture at that age, and avoiding the question increases fear.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old has a 2 cm scalp laceration from a fall. LET gel has been on for 25 minutes. What is the likely benefit?
choices: The wound may be repairable with no injected anesthetic at all
The wound no longer requires irrigation
Tetanus status no longer needs to be checked
Sedation is now mandatory before the repair
quiz.why: LET applied for 20-30 minutes often makes a small facial or scalp laceration repairable without injection, and where injection is still needed the needle passes through numb skin. Topical anesthesia does not replace irrigation, tetanus assessment or change sedation requirements.

quiz.q: A 2-month-old requires procedural sedation and the provider is considering ketamine. What is the relevant caution?
choices: Ketamine causes profound hypotension in infants
Ketamine is generally avoided under about 3 months of age
Ketamine has no reversal agent so it is never used in children
Ketamine is contraindicated in any child under 5 years
quiz.why: Ketamine is generally avoided below roughly 3 months, and laryngospasm is the complication to be set up for in young children. It tends to support blood pressure rather than drop it, and it is widely used in older children despite having no reversal agent.

quiz.q: A patient is going to the operating room for a testicular torsion. Which access should you anticipate for a case that might bleed significantly?
choices: One 22 gauge peripheral IV
A single 20 gauge IV plus a saline lock
Two large-bore IVs, roughly 14-18 gauge
No IV, since anesthesia will place one
quiz.why: Two large-bore lines allow rapid volume and blood delivery for anything that might bleed. Small-gauge catheters limit flow rates badly, and waiting for anesthesia to place access loses time the surgical patient does not have.

quiz.q: You are drawing a type and screen specimen at the bedside. Where and when is the tube labeled?
choices: At the nursing station, after all tubes for that patient are collected
In the hallway on the way to the tube system
By the lab, using the electronic order
At the bedside, in the patient's presence, before you leave the room
quiz.why: Blood bank tubes are labeled at the bedside with the patient present and two identifiers, because a mislabeled tube is how a patient receives the wrong blood. Labeling anywhere else breaks the chain of identity, and the lab cannot verify who the blood actually came from.

quiz.q: After removing a splint at 14:22 for reported numbness, which documentation entry meets the standard?
choices: 1420: patient reported numbness of the right index and middle fingers; 1422: splint removed; sensation returned to baseline; radial pulse 2+, cap refill under 2 sec; RN notified 1423
The splint was applied too tightly by the previous shift
Patient complained of numbness; splint issue resolved
Numbness reported; will monitor
quiz.why: A record is time-stamped, factual and complete enough that someone who was not there can reconstruct events, including the repeat neurovascular check and who was notified. Blame is an opinion that belongs nowhere in a chart, and vague entries document neither the finding nor the action.
